newsitem.title: INDIA: India's striking truck owners, government in talks.
newsitem.headline: India's striking truck owners, government in talks.

text.p: India's striking truck owners kept more than two million vehicles off the roads for a seventh day on Monday as they struggled with the government to find a solution to the crippling stoppage.
Economists and industry leaders said the strike was hitting the economy hard, paralysing trade, pushing up prices and affecting people's livelihoods.

Economist Kulbir Singh of the Institute of Economic Studies said the strike, which began on April 1 in protest over a proposed five percent service tax and a sharp rise in insurance premiums, was costing the country 10 billion rupees ($280 million) a day.
"Sincere efforts were on from both sides to come to an amicable solution," Chittranjan Dass, secretary-general of the All-India Motor Transport Congress (AIMTC), said in a statement.
"Discussions and talks are going on at different levels."
"The government is open to talks," a government spokesman told a briefing.
However, AIMTC spokesman S.P. Singh said the strike would continue until the proposed service tax was abandoned.
Finance Minister P. Chidambaram proposed the tax on road transport in the federal budget for the 1997/98 (April-March) financial year.
However, it is now unclear if the budget will be passed before a confidence vote in Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's ruling coalition government on Friday.

An AIMTC official, who asked not to be identified, told Reuters, "If there is no budget, there is no reason to continue the strike because if there is no finance bill, there is no proposition for the service tax."
The transport body is also protesting against a sharp rise in insurance premiums.
"The issue of insurance is likely to be resolved earlier than the service tax," Singh said.
AIMTC representatives had met parliament's finance panel to discuss their demands, he said.
Small transporters who own one or two trucks constitute 93 percent of the country's fleet.
Earlier on Sunday, the AIMTC officials sought guidance from political parties on how to break the deadlock. The politicians were hopeful a solution could be found soon, Singh said.

The government has offered to refer the rise in insurance premiums to the tariff advisory panel. "We have told the tariff advisory committee we will hold discussions with them," a senior government official told Reuters.
At least 2.2 million trucks have been kept off the roads since the strike began.

"If the strike continues, it will have alarming repercussions leading to an acute shortage of essential commodities and a significant push to prices...," A.S. Kasliwal, president of the Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry, said in a statement.

"The entire market economy is getting shrunk due to the unimaginable losses suffered consequent to the unexpected strike...," Vijay Kalantri, of the All-India Association of Industries, said in a statement.
The government has said that since parliament is still considering the budget, it is for lawmakers to decide whether to drop the proposed service tax. ($1 = 35.8 rupees)
